titles.l2: Building a square with odd numbers

kernelIdea: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², proved by induction; the algebra k² + 2k + 1 = (k+1)² is the entire inductive step.

kernels.l1: Odd numbers make square shells. Add the next shell and you still have a square.
kernels.l2: Adding up odd numbers always gives a square number. You can see why with tiles: each odd number is exactly the L-shaped shell that grows a square by one.
kernels.l3: Adding the first n odd numbers always gives n × n. The reason is that each odd number is the L-shaped shell that turns one square into the next, and the domino argument makes that a proof.
kernels.l4: The sum of the first n odd numbers equals n². The inductive step is the identity k² + (2k+1) = (k+1)², and the L-shell picture is the same fact drawn.
kernels.l5: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n². Induction proves it, and the whole step is one piece of algebra: k² plus the next odd number is (k+1)². The proof has to run forwards from that left side, not backwards from the answer.
kernels.l6: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², and the whole inductive step is the identity k² + (2k+1) = (k+1)². Writing it correctly means starting from the left side of the case you are proving and using the case before it — never manipulating the goal until something true appears.
kernels.l7: The first n odd numbers add up to n squared, proved by induction, where the whole step is the expansion of (k+1) squared. The argument has to run forwards from the case for k+1, never backwards from the goal.
kernels.l8: The identity is the n = 2 case of a family of power sums expressible by Faulhaber’s formula; the L-shell picture is a bijective proof of the same statement.

kernel: Σ from j = 1 to n of (2j − 1) equals n², proved by induction, written in the house style. The algebra k² + 2k + 1 = (k+1)² is the entire inductive step.
